| [LIT-1004](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1004.md) | Epistemic Injustice: Power and the Ethics of Knowing | Fricker (2007). Names two kinds of wrong done to someone in their capacity as a knower. Testimonial injustice: a speaker gets less credibility than the evidence warrants because of a prejudice about who they are. Hermeneutical injustice: a group's experience is hard to make sense of, for them and others, because the shared interpretive resources lack the concepts, and the gap traces to their marginalisation. Proposes testimonial and hermeneutical justice as corrective virtues. Held here for what it is standardly cited for; not read. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-12 from its Crossref record, not read. | [LIT-1005](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1005.md) | Social Cognitive Theory: An Agentic Perspective | Bandura (2001). Social cognitive theory's account of people as agents of their own functioning, not only products of their circumstances. The core features of agency are intentionality, forethought, self- reactiveness and self-reflectiveness, and beliefs of self-efficacy are the foundation of it. Distinguishes three modes: direct personal agency, proxy agency through others who act on one's behalf, and collective agency through shared beliefs in a group's efficacy. | [LIT-1006](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1006.md) | Living without Free Will | Pereboom (2001). Defends hard incompatibilism: whether determinism is true or not, we lack the free will that basic-desert moral responsibility requires. Its four-case argument runs from an agent manipulated moment by moment by neuroscientists, through programming and upbringing, to ordinary determinism. The cases do not differ in any way that matters to responsibility, so if the manipulated agent is not responsible, neither is the determined one. The record already meets the argument secondhand ([LIT-294](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-294.md), [LIT-684](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-684.md), [LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md)). | [LIT-1007](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1007.md) | The Ethics of Manipulation | Noggle, SEP (2018, revised 2026). A survey of what manipulation is and what makes it wrong. It sets out accounts on which manipulation bypasses or subverts rational capacities, accounts on which it is a kind of trickery that leads someone away from ideal norms of belief, desire or emotion, and accounts that treat it as pressure. It discusses how manipulation differs from persuasion and from coercion, and whether its wrong lies in harm, in disrespect for autonomy, or in the character of the manipulator. | [LIT-1009](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1009.md) | Sense of agency in the human brain | Haggard (2017). A review of the sense of agency, the experience of controlling one's own actions and through them events in the world. It sets prediction-based (comparator) accounts against retrospective, inferential ones and reviews implicit measures such as intentional binding, the compression of the perceived interval between an action and its outcome. It discusses the frontal and parietal circuits implicated, and what the sense of agency implies for responsibility. | [LIT-1010](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1010.md) | Relational Autonomy: Feminist Perspectives on Autonomy, Agency, and the Social Self | Mackenzie and Stoljar, eds. (2000). The collection that gave "relational autonomy" its name: an umbrella for views on which persons are socially embedded, and their identities and capacities for self-government are formed by social relations. The essays take up the feminist charge that standard conceptions of autonomy are individualistic, and ask whether oppressive socialisation undermines autonomy. They divide over whether an account should be procedural or must make substantive normative demands.
